new_people.name: Thomas Glasgow of Quothquan, 1527/28
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
7 February 1527/28: Thomas Gleschow is listed with Quothquan tenants fined for nonappearance in a case concerning breach of the lord’s judicial prohibition (called his “fence” in the text). The heading says 1527; Dickinson’s Appendix B assigns the court to 1527/28.<ref>William Croft Dickinson (ed.), Court Book of the Barony of Carnwath 1523–1542 (1937), printed pp.64–65, index p.217; Appendix B p.cxx; PDF 193–194; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=193. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

The remaining Thomas passages belong to five court meetings in all: 7 and 23 February 1527/28, 10 March 1527/28, 27 March 1528 and 20 May 1528. The February and 10 March meetings are entered twice. At the 27 March court Thomas is included in the tenant group adjudged to have broken two judicial prohibitions: cultivating Newmains while restricted and paying rents out despite an arrestment. Fines and imprisonment for a year at the lord’s will were decreed; actual imprisonment is not established. These proceedings name no Glasgow relative.<ref>Dickinson (1937), printed pp.64–70,79–88; Appendix B p.cxx; PDF193–199,208–217,125; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=214. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The tenant list begins “in Quodquen” on p.64; Thomas Gleschow falls before the separate Carswell names on p.65. This supports Quothquan itself, not merely the broad barony. John and Thomas form a plausible local family group, with their degree of kinship unknown. [[Glasgow-1095|John Glasgow]] is the leading possible existing-profile comparison for the Quothquan John, not a proved identification or parent of Thomas.



The five meetings are treated as one tenant’s career. The rolls do not identify his exact individual holding or establish that he inherited from John. Leases and tenancy succession might identify kin. No compatible existing profile was found in the bounded duplicate audit; the Dublin 1725 and Calton 1886 Thomas accounts have incompatible chronologies.

== Biography ==

Sarah Glasgow was a daughter of [[Glasgow-428|William Glasgow]] of Currituck, North Carolina. Her father named her in his will of 30 September 1746, proved 7 April 1747.<ref name="William1746">[https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/wills/glasgowwilliam1746.html William Glasgow will, 30 September 1746; proved 7 April 1747, North Carolina State Archives MARS 12.96.1.805; NCGenWeb published transcription checked 17 October 2026].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Her mother, exact dates and later identity remain unknown. The will names her paternal siblings Caleb, Abiah and Elizabeth; the identification of the adult Caleb profiles remains probable. The unnamed grandfather and the wife’s unborn child are not assigned modern identities. The contingent land interest and cattle in a mark given by an unnamed grandfather belong to Sarah’s bequest; the will does not name that grandfather. The account is based on the checked published transcription; the manuscript has not been newly inspected.

new_people.name: Alexander Elder
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The published headstone transcription for Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church records a memorial erected by Alexander Elder of Gortrickey to his father Robert Elder, his mother Jane, and his sisters and brothers. It also records Alexander Elder's death on 5 January 1943.<ref>Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church headstones; https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/graveyard.html; . This is a new direct memorial transcription for the catalogue's parentage study, not a Glasgow record and not proof that the Elder family was related to Alexander Glasgow. Its value is locality context: Gortrickey/Gortereghy is the townland where the Glasgow family appears in the 1837–1838 Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism entries. The memorial supplies a named Elder household for future comparison with the later Robert Elder who occupied Alexander Glasgow's former Lisnagaver lot; identity between those Elder references remains unproved.</ref>

A 2007 RootsChat research post reproduces a 18 June 1908 Second Portglenone Presbyterian marriage entry for Alexander Elder, full-age bachelor farmer of Gortreaghy, whose father is recorded as Robert Elder, farmer. Alexander married Mary Anderson, full-age spinster of Gortreaghy, daughter of Neil Anderson; witnesses were Robert Anderson and Margaret Elder.<ref>RootsChat, Elder, Murdoch & McMeekin Families; https://www.rootschat.com/forum/index.php?topic=214109.0; . The entry is not yet an inspected original, so it is a secondary-source lead rather than final evidence. It is nevertheless a new, specific parent-bearing record for the Gortreaghy Elder household and gives a testable route for determining whether the Alexander Elder on the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial was a son of the Robert Elder who later occupied Alexander Glasgow's Lisnagaver lot. That identity chain remains unproved.</ref>

The inspected original 1911 Gortereghy census return records Alexander Elder, aged 40, as head, Mary Elder, aged 44, as wife, Robert Elder, aged 34, as brother, and Margaret Elder, aged 25, as sister (Form A, official index house 37, nai001390156, rows 1–4). These stated relationships support comparison with the 1901 household, the 1908 marriage lead and the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial; identification with existing profiles remains qualified.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 Gortereghy return records Robert Elder, 65, widowed farmer, with Alex 27 and Robert 20 as sons and Eliza 22 and Margaretta 14 as daughters. The 1911 Alexander/Mary household explicitly records Robert as Alexander’s brother and Margaret as his sister. The combined names and locality strongly support continuity, with age differences retained. Robert [[Elder-7144]] remains a qualified father identity; Robert/Mary Glasgow’s Gortahar household is separate.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Robert Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298460.pdf; Form A; official index house 42; rows 1–5; 1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Identity revalidation, 17 October 2026: The original 1901 Alex is explicitly Robert’s son; the 1911 return names brother Robert and sister Margaret. Together with the 1908 Alexander/Mary Anderson marriage extract, these support one sibling family. Retain the actual age differences. Use the same qualified Elder-7144 father hypothesis for Alexander and proved siblings; mother Jane on the memorial is separately evidenced, while Jane Calderwood remains a comparison. No matching Alexander profile was established in full same-name and father-filtered searches.

new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
Nicholas Glasco is named in a 20 June 1746 report in the ''Weekly Worcester Journal'' among officers in the rebel army committed to New Gaol, Southwark. The notice lists him between John Duncan and Alexander M'Laughlan. It gives no rank for Nicholas individually and does not state a conviction, birthplace, residence, relatives, occupation, or dates of birth or death.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1214317653/ ''Weekly Worcester Journal'', 20 June 1746, p.4], original roster inspected 4 October 2026. Date follows provider metadata; masthead date has not been separately checked.</ref>


The 27 and 28 June reports describe Nicholas Glascoe as a self-styled major and allege a role in the attack on the Hazard sloop. These are allegations, not a finding of guilt.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394536822/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-06-27, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404059808/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-06-28, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

An August report lists Nicholas among persons indicted for high treason, while the 7 November paper announces the pending trial.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404060798/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-08-23, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394542827/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-11-07, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

The 8 and 17 November reports say he was acquitted, with defence evidence identifying him as a French native born at Saint-Germain-en-Laye and a lieutenant in Dillon’s Regiment. They report an order to detain him as a French prisoner. The Caledonian account also mentions a Not Guilty verdict and removal of his bolts; the saved excerpt stops before the full cartel articles. These reports require comparison with the underlying legal and military records.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404061824/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-11-08, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394462695/ The Caledonian Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

In May 1747 a notice names Mr Glascoe as major in Lord Ogilvy’s new regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate, but the missing forename and unproved continuity prevent a firm identification.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404076485/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1747-05-09, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

No parents, spouse, children, birth date, death date or Irish origin is established.

Further original issues preserve June rosters, indictment reprints and Dutch reports, along with acquittal reports containing translated cartel articles. These are related issue appearances; no independent family identity follows. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979338930/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury (The Sherborne Mercury, or Weekly Advertiser), 1746-06-30, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334222061/ S Gravenhaegse Courant, 1746-09-21, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979339079/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971385255/ The Gloucester Journal, 1746-11-18, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334158733/ Opregte Haarlemsche Courant, 1746-12-01, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

The Gloucester Journal of 28 April 1747 describes Major Glascoe as lately discharged at London and chief major in Lord Ogilvy’s projected regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate; no forename is given, and English pay is not interpreted as British military service.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971516263/ Gloucester Journal, 28 April 1747, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The rare full name, Southwark proceedings and Hazard episode support a probable association across the 1746 reports. French birth and service are reported defence evidence. They do not establish an Irish origin, a Glasgow-family connection or relatives. The May 1747 appointment lacks a forename.
